UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S RULE 54(b) MOTION TO VACATE ECF NO. 96 AND DETERMINE MAGISTRATE JUDGE DAVIS’S OWNERSHIP OF META COMMON STOCK

I.	INTRODUCTION

ECF No. 86 asked one question of fact: whether Magistrate Judge Davis held common stock of Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) while he entered orders in this action. ECF No. 86 at 2. ECF No. 96 answered a different question. It held that reassignment made the motion moot. ECF No. 96 at 1. The question of fact was never decided.

Reassignment ended Magistrate Judge Davis’s participation. It did not change whether he owned Meta stock on September 9, 2026, when he entered ECF No. 64, or on October 7, 2026, when he entered ECF No. 84. Those two orders remain in force. A pending application before the District Judge, ECF No. 93, seeks relief from them on the ground that § 455 required disqualification when they were entered. The ownership facts are the predicate of that application. A disposition that declared the request for those facts moot, without finding them and without providing for their development, is the error this Motion asks the Court to correct.

The Motion asks for three things in sequence. First, vacatur of ECF No. 96 under Rule 54(b). Second, restoration of the historical component of ECF No. 86 for decision. Third, a decision: a finding that Magistrate Judge Davis owned Meta common stock on the two dates or, in the alternative, an on-record determination of who owned the reported asset on each date and whether it was a financial interest under § 455(d)(4), after the factual development needed to answer. The Motion asks the Court to decide the question. It does not ask the Court to reserve it again.

II.	STATEMENT OF FACTS

A. The reports. Exhibit A to ECF No. 86 is the Financial Disclosure Report (AO Form 10) of “Davis, Ivan,” Magistrate Judge, U.S. District Court, Virginia Eastern, for calendar year 2025. ECF No. 86-2. It bears two electronic signatures, May 14, 2026 and May 26, 2026. ECF No. 86-2 at 2 (report page 1). Part VII, line 6, reads “FB common stock.” ECF No. 86-2 at 3 (report page 2). ECF No. 86 describes line 6 as reporting a gross year-end value of $15,001 to $50,000, dividend income of $1,000 or less, and no transaction. ECF No. 86 at 2; ECF No. 87 at 2. Exhibit B is the Financial Disclosure Report of “Davis, Ivan D.,” U.S. Magistrate Judge, full-time, for calendar year 2024, dated August 18, 2025. ECF No. 86-3 at 2 (report page 1). Part VII, line 6, reads “FB common stock,” income code A, income type “Dividend,” value code K, value method T. ECF No. 86-3 at 5 (report page 4). The report’s legend defines code A as $1,000 or less and code K as $15,001 to $50,000. ECF No. 87 at 2. Line 6 reports no transaction. Each report carries the filer’s certification that the information given, “including information pertaining to my spouse and minor or dependent children, if any,” is “accurate, true, and complete to the best of my knowledge and belief.” ECF No. 86-2 at 2; ECF No. 86-3 at 9 (report page 8).

Both reports identify common-stock holdings by trading symbol. Both list mutual funds and exchange-traded funds as separate line items. Both list an individual retirement account as a separate line item. ECF No. 87 at 3. “FB” was the Nasdaq trading symbol of the Class A common stock of Facebook, Inc. Facebook, Inc. changed its name to Meta Platforms, Inc. on October 28, 2021. The trading symbol changed to “META” in June 2022. ECF No. 86 at 2–3; ECF No. 87 at 3 (identifying the public filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission).

This Memorandum cites the reports by ECF attachment page, with the report’s internal page in parentheses. ECF Nos. 86 and 87 cite the same pages by internal page (“Ex. A at 2,” “Ex. B at 4”). The two systems refer to the same pages.

B. The orders. Meta has been a defendant since July 30, 2026. ECF Nos. 1, 5. Meta appeared and moved to dismiss on August 21, 2026. ECF Nos. 21, 22, 24. Magistrate Judge Davis entered ECF No. 64 on September 9, 2026. It required Plaintiff to file by September 11, 2026 a redlined comparison of the proposed Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint against the original Complaint. ECF No. 64 at 1. He entered ECF No. 84 on October 7, 2026. It denied ECF No. 15, which sought leave to serve three interrogatories on NCMEC, and ECF No. 54, which sought leave to serve four interrogatories on Meta, as premature. It denied ECF No. 59, the motion for leave to amend, for noncompliance with ECF No. 64. ECF No. 84 at 1–2.

C. The October 13 filings. On October 13, 2026, Plaintiff filed three coordinated applications, each entered October 14, 2026. ECF No. 86 moved before Magistrate Judge Davis under § 455(b)(4) and § 455(a). It asked the Court to “state on the record” the five facts quoted in the Motion at paragraph 7, and to disqualify upon those facts. ECF No. 86 at 4–6. It stated that the companion filings “seek the retrospective and case-management remedies” and that “[t]his Motion does not.” ECF No. 86 at 5. ECF Nos. 89–91 presented Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 84 before the District Judge. ECF Nos. 93–94 moved before the District Judge for targeted vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84 and withdrawal or modification of the referral. ECF No. 93 ¶ 5 identified the questions requiring resolution: “whether the reported interest is a covered financial interest; the arrangement through which it is held and whether 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4)(i) applies; the dates of ownership; knowledge, where § 455(b)(4) requires it; and whether the conditions of 28 U.S.C. § 455(f) are satisfied.” Its request R2 sought vacatur “upon the statutory findings identified in paragraph 5.” ECF No. 93 ¶ 10(R2).

D. ECF No. 96 and the reassignment. On October 22, 2026, an unnumbered docket entry recorded: “Case Reassigned to Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick. Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis no longer assigned to the case.” The same day, Magistrate Judge Davis signed ECF No. 96. It states that the matter “can be resolved without oral argument.” It orders: “Plaintiff’s Motion is DENIED AS MOOT. The case has been reassigned to Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick.” ECF No. 96 at 1. It contains no finding on any item in ECF No. 86, Part V.

E. ECF Nos. 97–99. On October 23, 2026, Plaintiff filed Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 96 before the District Judge. ECF Nos. 97, 98, 99. Objection One contends that the reassignment may have ended the authority to adjudicate ECF No. 86 before ECF No. 96 was entered. ECF No. 97 ¶¶ 7–10. Objection Two contends that ECF No. 96 may have exceeded the administrative action permitted after a recusal or during a period of required disqualification. ECF No. 97 ¶¶ 11–13. ECF Nos. 97–99 also request identification of the authority and procedure that produced the successor designation. ECF No. 97 ¶ 15; ECF No. 99 at 10–11. Those filings state that Plaintiff “raises no objection to Magistrate Judge Fitzpatrick personally.” ECF No. 97 ¶ 16. As alternative relief, ECF No. 99 asked the District Judge to decide ECF No. 93 “on its own grounds, resolving the statutory facts to the extent necessary to that decision.” ECF No. 99 at 11. It stated that Plaintiff “does not ask the Court to restore every determination requested in ECF No. 86 as a standalone controversy” and that “[t]he determinations necessary to that relief belong in the District Judge’s resolution of the pending applications, on an appropriate factual record.” ECF No. 99 at 11. Part IV.E of this Memorandum addresses the relationship between that request and this Motion.

III.	THE GOVERNING STANDARD

A. Rule 54(b). An order that adjudicates fewer than all the claims “may be revised at any time before the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims and all the parties’ rights and liabilities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). A district court “retains the power to reconsider and modify its interlocutory judgments . . . at any time prior to final judgment when such is warranted.” Am. Canoe Ass’n v. Murphy Farms, Inc., 326 F.3d 505, 514–15 (4th Cir. 2003). The discretion “is not limitless.” Carlson v. Boston Scientific Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). A court may revise an interlocutory order under the same circumstances in which it may depart from the law of the case: “a subsequent trial produc[ing] substantially different evidence,” a change in applicable law, or “clear error causing ‘manifest injustice.’” Id. The Fourth Circuit restated the three grounds in Clear Touch Interactive, Inc. v. The Ockers Co., Nos. 25-1304 & 25-1374, slip op. at 22–25 & n.6 (4th Cir. Apr. 1, 2026) (published), and affirmed a revision that corrected a legal error in a prior interlocutory ruling. Clear Touch predates ECF No. 96. Plaintiff cites it for the Rule 54(b) standard, not as an intervening change in law.

B. The successor judge. Where “the order was entered by one judge and then reviewed by another,” the latter judge “should be hesitant to overrule the earlier determination.” Carlson, 856 F.3d at 325. In U.S. Tobacco Coop. Inc. v. Big South Wholesale of Va., LLC, 899 F.3d 236, 256–60 (4th Cir. 2018), the Fourth Circuit vacated a successor district judge’s reconsideration of a predecessor’s substitution order because the successor neither identified one of the three grounds nor could have satisfied the clear-error ground on that record. The court repeated that a prior decision qualifies for the third ground only if it was “dead wrong.” Id. at 258 (quoting TFWS, Inc. v. Franchot, 572 F.3d 186, 194 (4th Cir. 2009)). U.S. Tobacco rejected a reconsideration that did not satisfy the governing grounds. It did not hold that a predecessor’s ruling is beyond correction when a ground is satisfied. Clear Touch applied the same standard and upheld the correction of a legal error by a judge who had inherited the case from a colleague. Slip op. at 24–25 & n.6.

C. The magistrate judge’s authority. A district judge “may designate a magistrate judge to hear and determine any pretrial matter pending before the court,” subject to the exceptions listed in the statute. 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). In this District, “[d]uties and cases may be assigned or referred to a magistrate judge by an order entered in the action or on the instructions of a district judge.” Local Civil Rule 72. The District Judge may reconsider a magistrate judge’s pretrial order “where it has been shown that the magistrate judge’s order is clearly erroneous or contrary to law.” 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A); Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a). ECF No. 96 was entered within the referral of pretrial matters. The successor magistrate judge now holds that referral. A Rule 54(b) motion to revise a pretrial order entered within the referral is itself a pretrial matter within it.

IV.	ARGUMENT

A.	ECF No. 96 Determined That Reassignment Mooted ECF No. 86 in Its Entirety, and That Determination Is Subject to Revision Under Rule 54(b).

ECF No. 96 made one legal determination. It determined that reassignment rendered ECF No. 86 moot in its entirety. ECF No. 96 at 1. That determination disposed of every request in ECF No. 86, including the Part V and Request A2 requests for findings of fact. It is an interlocutory order. No judgment has been entered. Rule 54(b) permits its revision. Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b); Am. Canoe, 326 F.3d at 514–15.

Plaintiff asks the Court to reconsider that determination on the third Carlson ground. The asserted error is legal. It is the effect given to reassignment on a pending request for historical findings. ECF No. 96 made no finding on ownership, holding arrangement, or divestiture. The reconsideration requested here therefore involves no reweighing of a predecessor’s factual finding. It involves review of a legal conclusion about mootness.

Plaintiff maintains, in ECF Nos. 97–99, the objection that Magistrate Judge Davis may have lacked authority to enter ECF No. 96 after the reassignment. ECF No. 97 ¶¶ 7–10. This Motion does not abandon that objection. The two are alternatives. If ECF No. 96 was entered without authority, the District Judge may vacate it on that ground under Rule 72(a). If it was entered with authority, it is an interlocutory order within the referral that the assigned magistrate judge may revise under Rule 54(b). Either route reaches the same order.

B.	Reassignment Mooted the Prospective Requests. It Did Not Moot the Request for Historical Findings.

A matter is moot when an intervening event makes it impossible for the court to grant “any effectual relief whatever” to the requesting party. Church of Scientology of Cal. v. United States, 506 U.S. 9, 12 (1992). The availability of a partial remedy is enough to prevent mootness. Id. at 12–13.

ECF No. 86 presented two kinds of requests. The prospective requests sought to end Magistrate Judge Davis’s participation: disqualification, priority determination, and transfer of the referred matters. ECF No. 86 at 5–6 (Requests A1, A3, A4). Reassignment supplied that relief. Magistrate Judge Davis no longer participates. The prospective requests are moot.

The historical requests sought findings of fact. Part V asked the Court to “state on the record” whether the asset reported as “FB common stock” is Meta common stock, whether it was held on specified dates, the date and manner of any divestiture, and whether it is held directly or through a fund within § 455(d)(4)(i). ECF No. 86 at 4. Request A2 asked the Court to “[s]tate on the record whether the reported interest was held during the challenged participation.” ECF No. 86 at 6. Those requests concern completed events. Whether Magistrate Judge Davis owned Meta stock on September 9, 2026 and on October 7, 2026 is a fact fixed on those dates. Reassignment on October 22, 2026 did not alter it.

Effectual relief remains available on the historical requests. The findings were requested as relief in their own right: ECF No. 86 asked that they be stated “on the record.” ECF No. 86 at 4, 6. They are also the predicate of a pending application. ECF No. 93 seeks vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84 “upon the statutory findings identified in paragraph 5,” which include “the dates of ownership” and the holding arrangement. ECF No. 93 ¶¶ 5, 10(R2). ECF No. 93 ¶ 10(R7) requests a decision record identifying “the period for which [the disqualification ground] is established.” Findings entered on the restored request would become part of the record in this action. They would be available to the District Judge when he decides ECF No. 93. A request whose grant produces findings that a pending application requires is not a request on which no effectual relief can follow.

ECF No. 96 did not distinguish the two kinds of requests. It treated reassignment as disposing of all of them. ECF No. 96 at 1. Reassignment answered the prospective requests only. The determination that it mooted the historical requests was error.

C.	The Error Causes Manifest Injustice Because ECF No. 96 Terminated a Requested Historical Inquiry While Its Subject Remains Material to a Pending Statutory Challenge.

The injustice is traced to ECF No. 96 itself. ECF No. 96 closed the proceeding in which Plaintiff expressly requested determination of the reported financial interest. It did so without deciding ownership and without providing for development of the ownership record. ECF Nos. 64 and 84 remain operative. ECF No. 84 denied leave to amend and denied the discovery motions directed to NCMEC and Meta. ECF No. 84 at 1–2. ECF No. 93 presents a statutory challenge to both orders that depends on the ownership facts. ECF No. 93 ¶¶ 5, 10(R2). Terminating the historical inquiry as moot, while its subject remains material to that pending challenge, leaves the challenge without the findings it requires and leaves the orders in force without any officer having determined the fact on which their validity under § 455 is questioned.

Plaintiff does not contend that an unfavorable order causes manifest injustice by being unfavorable. Plaintiff does not reargue here whether ECF Nos. 64 and 84 were correct when entered. Those questions are presented in ECF Nos. 66, 67, 89–91, and 93. The point here is narrower. The pending district-judge applications preserve additional means of correction. They do not supply the determination requested in ECF No. 86. ECF No. 99 asked the District Judge to resolve the statutory facts “to the extent necessary” to ECF No. 93. ECF No. 99 at 11. That request is conditional on the District Judge’s path to decision. ECF No. 86 requested the findings unconditionally, as relief. ECF No. 96 ended that request without reaching it.

D.	The Successor-Judge Restraint Does Not Bar Correction of a Legal Error in a Mootness Ruling That Made No Finding.

Carlson counsels hesitation where one judge’s order is reviewed by another. 856 F.3d at 325. U.S. Tobacco enforces that restraint: a successor may not revisit a predecessor’s factual determinations on a “blanket de novo review.” 899 F.3d at 258–59. Plaintiff accepts both. The restraint protects a predecessor’s determinations from re-weighing. ECF No. 96 made a legal determination about mootness and no factual determination about ownership. Correcting the mootness ruling disturbs no finding. It reaches a request that was never decided.

The error also meets the standard U.S. Tobacco applies. A mootness ruling is legal. The test is whether any effectual relief remained available. Church of Scientology, 506 U.S. at 12. Effectual relief remained available on the historical requests for the reasons stated in Part IV.B. A disposition that treats a live request for historical findings as mooted by a change in future assignment does not survive that test. Clear Touch confirms that a successor judge acts within Rule 54(b) when he corrects a legal error in an interlocutory ruling he inherited. Slip op. at 24–25 & n.6.

Plaintiff does not argue the ownership evidence as a reason to reconsider. The reports were before the Court when ECF No. 96 issued. ECF Nos. 86-2, 86-3. They are not new evidence. The ground for reconsideration is the legal effect given to reassignment. The evidence bears on the second stage, the decision of the restored request, addressed in Part IV.F.

E.	The Requested Determination Is Within the Referral, and It Is an Additional Request That Does Not Conflict With ECF No. 99.

The referral authorizes the magistrate judge to “hear and determine any pretrial matter pending before the court.” 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). ECF No. 86 was such a matter. It was filed before the magistrate judge, decided by the magistrate judge, and is now presented for revision to the magistrate judge who holds the referral. The findings requested are findings on a referred pretrial motion. They are not advisory because the officer who makes them does not also decide every consequence that follows from them. Section 636 and Rule 72 contemplate magistrate-judge adjudication and fact development within a district-court proceeding, subject to the District Judge’s review. 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A); Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a). Findings entered on the restored request become part of the record in this action. The District Judge may consider them in resolving ECF No. 93. That use does not convert this Motion into a proceeding under Rule 72(b), and Plaintiff does not ask the Court to label the findings a report and recommendation. The request is for a decision within the restored pretrial proceeding. Rule 52(a)(3) dispenses with findings on most motions; it does not prohibit the factual determination requested here, which ECF No. 86 sought as its own relief.

Plaintiff states the relationship to ECF No. 99 directly. ECF No. 99 asked the District Judge to decide ECF No. 93 “on its own grounds, resolving the statutory facts to the extent necessary to that decision.” ECF No. 99 at 11. It stated that Plaintiff “does not ask the Court to restore every determination requested in ECF No. 86 as a standalone controversy” and that “[t]he determinations necessary to that relief belong in the District Judge’s resolution of the pending applications, on an appropriate factual record.” Id. That was an allocation of the ownership question to the District Judge’s decision of ECF No. 93, to the extent that decision required it. Plaintiff maintains that request.

This Motion is an additional procedural request now being made. It asks the assigned magistrate judge, as the officer holding the referral in which ECF No. 86 was filed and decided, to vacate the mootness disposition and decide the restored request. The two requests are consistent. Findings by the magistrate judge on the restored request would supply the “appropriate factual record” on which ECF No. 99 asked the District Judge to act. A decision here does not decide ECF No. 93. It does not resolve the objections pending before the District Judge. It decides what ECF No. 86 asked. ECF No. 86 was directed to the magistrate judge, and the magistrate judge decided it without reaching the question. The officer who now holds that referral is the officer positioned to decide the question in the first instance. This Motion confines the restored request to the two dates on which the orders challenged in ECF No. 93 were entered, so that the restored request asks no more than the pending application requires.

Plaintiff does not ask that the ownership question be left for possible later determination through the pending applications. Plaintiff asks that it be determined.

F.	The Reports Support the Requested Findings. If the Court Does Not Draw the Inference of Continued Personal Ownership, It Should Determine the Holder and the Statutory Classification on Each Date.

The requested findings are stated in the Motion at paragraph 17. The evidence for each follows.

Issuer. Both reports describe line 6 as “FB common stock.” ECF No. 86-2 at 3; ECF No. 86-3 at 5. Both reports identify common stock by trading symbol. ECF No. 87 at 3. “FB” was the Nasdaq trading symbol of the Class A common stock of Facebook, Inc., which changed its name to Meta Platforms, Inc. on October 28, 2021; the symbol changed to “META” in June 2022. ECF No. 86 at 2–3; ECF No. 87 at 3 (identifying the Form 8-K and Forms 10-K that establish those facts). The reports continue to use the former symbol. The description supports the finding that line 6 denotes common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.

Ownership on the two dates. The reports establish the reported holding at the close of 2024 and at the close of 2025. Each report places the holding in the same value range. Neither records a purchase or sale on line 6 during its reporting period. ECF No. 86-2 at 3; ECF No. 86-3 at 5. The 2025 report was certified on May 14 and May 26, 2026. ECF No. 86-2 at 2. The certification dates are not themselves evidence of ownership on those dates; they are evidence of when the year-end 2025 holding was reported. The reports do not directly document ownership on September 9 or October 7, 2026. They support an inference of continuity: an asset held at two consecutive year-ends, in the same value range, with no reported transaction, continued to be held nine and ten months later. Plaintiff advances continued ownership as that inference. ECF No. 86 at 3; ECF No. 93 ¶ 5. Plaintiff asks the Court to draw it and to enter findings (b) and (c). To the extent the Court requires more before drawing it, Part IV.G describes the record to be completed.

Statutory classification. Section 455(d)(4) defines “financial interest” as “ownership of a legal or equitable interest, however small.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4). The exception in § 455(d)(4)(i) applies to “[o]wnership in a mutual or common investment fund that holds securities.” The reports list line 6 as common stock. They list mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, and an individual retirement account as separate line items. ECF No. 87 at 3. On the face of the reports, line 6 is a direct holding. Finding (d) follows from findings (a) through (c) and from the face of the reports, subject to the holding-arrangement fact addressed below.

The holder. The AO Form 10 certification covers “information pertaining to my spouse and minor or dependent children.” ECF No. 86-2 at 2; ECF No. 86-3 at 9. Line 6 does not state whose asset it is. Section 455(b)(4) reaches a financial interest held by the judge “individually or as a fiduciary, or his spouse or minor child residing in his household.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4). ECF No. 93 ¶ 5 did not allege ownership by the Magistrate Judge personally rather than by another covered holder. If the record shows that the asset was owned on either date by Magistrate Judge Davis as a fiduciary, by his spouse, or by a minor child residing in his household, Plaintiff requests that finding in place of findings (b) and (c). A dependent child listed on a disclosure form is not for that reason a minor child residing in the household within § 455(b)(4); the finding must identify the holder by the statutory category. Identification of the holder does not itself establish a violation. Knowledge under § 455(b)(4), the application of § 455(f), and the remedy for any order entered remain reserved to ECF No. 93. Motion ¶ 19.

The alternative request. If the Court does not accept the inference of continued personal ownership on the present record, Plaintiff requests an on-record determination whether the reported asset was owned on September 9 and October 7, 2026 by Magistrate Judge Davis or another holder covered by § 455(b)(4), and whether the interest fell within § 455(d)(4). Motion ¶ 20. That request does not depend on the Court accepting Plaintiff’s inference. It asks the Court to answer the question either way, after the development described next.

G.	The Court May Develop the Ownership Record Through a Procedure Within Its Authority Without Returning Any Adjudication to Magistrate Judge Davis.

Rule 43(c) provides that when a motion relies on facts outside the record, “the court may hear the matter on affidavits or may hear it wholly or partly on oral testimony or on depositions.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 43(c). The rule supplies a method for receiving evidence on a motion. It does not itself establish a successor magistrate judge’s power to compel another judicial officer to produce financial information, and Plaintiff does not cite it for that proposition.

Plaintiff proposes two sources and asks the Court to select the lawful procedure for obtaining them: a written statement from Magistrate Judge Davis addressing the four facts identified in the Motion at paragraph 21, and the records that show ownership of the reported asset on the two dates. Motion ¶ 22. The Court may request the statement. The Court may receive the records. The Court may set a date for the submission and a period for the parties’ responses. Plaintiff does not request a deposition of any judicial officer, general financial discovery, unrelated investment records, or any inquiry into judicial deliberations. Plaintiff does not request that nonresponse be treated as establishing ownership. Motion ¶ 22.

Historical facts about one judge’s participation can be developed before a different judge. In Liljeberg v. Health Services Acquisition Corp., 486 U.S. 847, 850–51 (1988), the court of appeals determined that resolution of a § 455 motion “required factual findings concerning the extent and timing of” the trial judge’s knowledge of a disqualifying interest and “remanded the matter to a different judge for such findings.” The different judge made them, and the case proceeded on that record. Id. at 851. Liljeberg arose on a Rule 60(b)(6) motion after final judgment, and its remedial holding is not invoked here. Plaintiff cites it for what its procedural history shows: a judge other than the one whose interest was questioned found the historical facts about that interest. That is the procedure requested.

Obtaining information from Magistrate Judge Davis is not returning adjudication to him. The restored request is to be decided by the assigned magistrate judge. Motion ¶ 23. The statement and records, if obtained, are evidence on a motion that another officer decides.

Disposition dates are part of that record. If the asset was sold or transferred before either date, the date of the sale or transfer establishes nonownership on that date. If it was sold or transferred after, the date establishes ownership through that point. Plaintiff requests those facts for that purpose. The application of § 455(f), which depends on additional conditions, remains reserved to ECF No. 93.

H.	The Requested Disposition.

Proposed Order A grants reconsideration, vacates ECF No. 96, restores the historical component of ECF No. 86, and enters the four findings on the existing record. It separates ownership on September 9 from ownership on October 7. It separates issuer identity, actual ownership, and statutory classification. It states that the findings become part of the record in this action and do not themselves decide the relief requested in ECF No. 93. It recognizes separately that prospective removal of Magistrate Judge Davis from further participation is unnecessary following reassignment.

Proposed Order B grants reconsideration, vacates ECF No. 96, restores the historical request for decision, and establishes a court-controlled procedure for obtaining the written statement, the records, or both, with a period for the parties to respond. It states the question to be determined so that it encompasses the actual holder and the statutory classification on each date, not only whether Plaintiff’s inference is correct. It retains the request for determination. Its submission and response periods are requested scheduling terms, not preexisting deadlines. It contains no provision closing ECF No. 86, denying the historical request without prejudice, or substituting preservation for adjudication.

Plaintiff also requests that the order disposing of this Motion state the disposition of the vacatur request, the requested ownership findings, and the alternative request for factual development and determination; and, for any request not reached, identify the ground on which the Court declines to reach it. Motion ¶ 27 (Seventh). That is a request concerning the form of the Court’s disposition. It is not an outcome Plaintiff offers as relief.

V.	CONCLUSION

ECF No. 96 determined that reassignment mooted ECF No. 86 in its entirety. Reassignment mooted the prospective requests. It did not moot the request for historical findings about ownership on September 9 and October 7, 2026, which remain the predicate of a pending statutory challenge to ECF Nos. 64 and 84. The determination was clear error, and terminating the historical inquiry on that ground, while its subject remains material, causes manifest injustice. The Court should vacate ECF No. 96, restore the historical component of ECF No. 86, and decide it: by entering the findings stated in the Motion at paragraph 17 or, in the alternative, by determining on a developed record who owned the reported asset on each date and whether it was a financial interest under § 455(d)(4). Plaintiff requests entry of Proposed Order A or, in the alternative, Proposed Order B.
